name: Serpent
lede: Serpent is a grayish green listed in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; nobody records who named it, but green has been the color of serpents in European imagery for centuries.

sections.title: A green with a snake's name
sections.body:
Serpent is a grayish green with a snake's name, and the name is nearly all the sources tell us. Our swatch, #647E74, comes from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, plate 29 D 5, which gives 1892 as its first recorded use [1]. The closest ISCC-NBS block is grayish green, 5.1 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale, and its Munsell notation is 8.4G 5.0/2.2 [1]. Who first used the word for a color, and why, is undocumented in the sources we hold [1].

Its nearest named colors are [[deep-bluish-grey-green]], [[deep-greyish-blue-green]], [[hydro]] and [[xanadu]] [1]. The nearest cut stone in our data is [[gem:turquoise|turquoise]], 6.8 units away [1]. A livelier cousin is [[sage]], and the plant-green family is described under [[moss]].

sections.title: The green of serpents
sections.body:
The color word is recent, but the pairing is old. Pastoureau writes that in the medieval bestiaries most serpents were green, and that the color marked an evil and dangerous nature, as with the asp, the viper and the dragon [2]. Satan's retinue divided into dark animals and green ones, and the green list ran from the dragon and serpent to the crocodile, hydra, basilisk, frog, siren and locust [2]. In miniatures, dragons are usually green and yellow, spotted and scaled to suggest a slimy, pustular body [2].

Green eyes belonged to the basilisk and to all serpents in the bestiaries [3]. The French saying that sets green eyes beside viper eyes is later: Pastoureau dates it only to the nineteenth century [3]. In his short book on color he adds that artists made demons, dragons and serpents greenish because green sat uneasily between this world and the next [5].

Jarman imagines the serpent of Eden camouflaged in green, khaki as the dust, and calls it the green devil [6]. Finlay's serpent is a different animal: the Rainbow Serpent of Aboriginal Australian stories, which in one tale swallows the Wawilak sisters, and is named for a rainbow rather than a single green [9].

sections.title: Why a duller green
sections.body:
The swatch is dull for a green: its chroma is 11.8, in the 15th percentile among the named colors in our data [1]. Pastoureau says medieval artists drew the viscous bodies of dragons and serpents with wavy lines, scaly partitions and desaturated greens [4]. In their eyes wetness meant lack of density, so draining the saturation from green or black made it look wetter [4]. Serpent sits at that dull end of the green range.

Pastoureau adds that recipe collections recommended sandragon, a red pigment named for dragon's blood, for painting the Devil's face and the flames of hell [2]. St Clair explains what it really was [10]. No animal is harmed in its making, because dragon's blood is a red resin drawn from wounded trees, often of the genus Dracaena [10].

sections.title: Legends with serpents in them
sections.body:
Two stories tie serpents to the history of color, and both are legends. The first is that murexide, a purple dye, came from the excrement of serpents. Garfield records that this was said, but its true source was bird droppings [7]. The second is that the German chemist Kekulé saw the ring of the benzene molecule in a dream of a serpent devouring its tail [8]. Ball calls the tale the stuff of legend and asks how much Kekulé embroidered it in his later accounts, noting that all we can be sure of is the published record [8].

A third, from Essex, is the pamphlet *The Flying Serpent* of 1669, which reported a winged dragon seen in Essex on 27 May 1668, with men from Saffron Walden going after it [10]. It is a report of a sighting, not a color source, and St Clair suggests it may have been a last-gasp appearance of a creature about to vanish into myth, and with it the dragon's blood pigment [10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 268 hold this green: within six units of CIEDE2000 and covering at least five per cent of the canvas, about 1.1 per cent of the archive [11]. These are museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [11].

Impressionism is where it concentrates: 10 of 140 Impressionist paintings in our data, and 4 of 45 Post-Impressionist ones [11]. [[painter:paul-cezanne|Cézanne]] has it in 9 of his 50 works here [11]. The canvases that hold the most are Caillebotte's [[painting:nga-66404|Skiffs]] of 1877, at 57 per cent, Klimt's [[painting:commons-Q28015487|Sunflower]] of 1907, at 53 per cent, and the Dutch seascape [[painting:smk-KMSsp537|Dutch Roadstead]] of 1638, at 47 per cent [11].

Its closest company in the data is [[viridian]], and the 1900s hold it at 2.4 times the archive rate, with 46 of 1,674 paintings [11]. Within a painting it is usually a mid-tone, in 47 per cent of cases, and a highlight in 37 per cent [11].

questions.q: What was dragon's blood, the pigment recommended for painting the Devil's face?
choices: A red resin from wounded trees
questions.answer: A red resin from wounded trees

questions.q: True or false: the purple dye murexide really came from the excrement of serpents.
Why did medieval artists use dull, desaturated greens for dragons and serpents?
choices: Desaturating a color made it look wetter and more viscous
questions.answer: Desaturating a color made it look wetter and more viscous

openers: In medieval bestiaries most serpents were green, and the color signaled an evil nature.
A dull, desaturated green was how medieval artists made dragons and serpents look wet and viscous.

issues: Removed the unsupported "greener and more iron-rich variety" description of turquoise.
Flying Serpent: sighting placed in Essex with Saffron Walden men in pursuit (St Clair), and the "last years of belief" claim softened to St Clair's own hedged suggestion.
Bestiary, green-eyes, viscous/desaturated, sandragon, murexide, Kekule and Rainbow Serpent claims traced to Pastoureau, Garfield, Ball, Finlay, St Clair: supported; legends already framed as legends.
Name origin is undocumented; stated as such. Chroma percentile is from our data, not a book.
